comments.author: glhaynes
comments.text:
I'd be really interested to see attitudes toward AI coding broken down by "has managerial experience" versus "doesn't". (No value judgment is held, expressed, or implied here.)

As someone with limited-but-not-no managerial experience, AI feels like a direct report, but one who mostly doesn't tune out if I give them a lot of context (unlike human direct reports), and thus I feel like I'm mostly getting exactly what I want — as long as I make some rational decisions about what it is I'm really after and where I draw the "here's where the returns start to diminish so we won't go further" line.

Anyway, it feels to me like it's ~as much a craft, just operating at a different level, much like how writing in a high-level language feels different from writing assembly. Enjoyed reading the post.

comments.author: sgreben
comments.text:
I'd be really interested to see attitudes toward AI coding broken down by "has managerial experience" versus "doesn't". (No value judgment is held, expressed, or implied here.)


I like this angle. Right now AI coding has a distinct management-like aesthetic, and it's often dramatically emphasized as well when people talk about it. Whether this aesthetic appeals to someone, or not, seems quite predictive of how they'll feel about AI dev overall.

Agentic dev, in the sense of "use requirement docs to box-in a set of LLMs-in-a-loop to produce the software you want", happens to be the first (and, arguably most immediate/obvious) approach that is useful and attractive enough (to enough people, and to the right set of people) - and I suspect that the implicit fear/status dimension here contributes a lot to its adoption right now (including reluctant adoption).

I don't think that this is the end state of building software with LLMs though - there has not been all that much time to figure out how to build on top of what-LLMs-are (and also what to build that way), so I'd be surprised if the current set of approaches was already exhaustive.

comments.author: natano
comments.text:
I don't think human coding will ever go away.

Here is my reasoning for it, but be warned; it somehow gets into the predicting-the-future/crystal-ball territory.
If that doesn't deter you from reading it anyway: Let's go!




In the not-so-distant future, there will be many companies where none of the employees (coders/programmers/AI-users?) understand the product anymore, because it was vibecoded. Some breaking bug comes up, that the slop-machine can't fix and some human has to dig into the code, understand what's going on and fix the bug. This will open up the market for human coding consultants/freelancers to offer their services. Given, that this will be a niche market, because most people jumped on the AI-bandwagon, it will be well paid.




Not everyone buys into the output quality (or lack thereof) of coding agents. Going with the IKEA analogy brought up in the article: Not everyone wants to have a house full of IKEA furniture. There are still people hiring carpenters to create furniture for them. Granted, there are less carpenters around than before the industrial/IKEA era, but the ones that do still exist have a queue of commissions and are doing quite well for themselves. (At least in the area where I live.)




There are sensitive occupational areas, where you can't leave code quality up to chance. e.g. space travel, military applications, law and medical applications. In those areas letting an AI agent introduce bugs into your codebase can be much more costly, than just hiring humans that will code by hand, come up with appropriate tests, perform simulations and fuzz test the application. Explody rocket bad. In those cases AI might (and probably will, or already is) used for additional quality assurance.




Writing code is a fun sparetime activity. If you are not pushed to perform by some employer or have to use the latest shiny new technology/framework/whatever, it can be quite fulfilling.




Someone has to write the code that future AI systems will be trained on. 🤡



There will be less people who know how to code, but it will still be useful and profitable.
I will certainly not stop coding anytime soon.

comments.author: pkd
comments.text:
I think this transition from vocation to craftsmanship will take at least 10 years, if not more. If we take mid-2025 as the baseline, I expect that by sometime in 2036, programming would have become mostly commoditised.

Why 10 years? I think people need to see the evidence that LLM-coded products are reliable-ish over a long period of time, that they don't continue to cause security incidents at the same rate over time, that the price of LLM-generated code does not start creeping up after wide adoption, etc. Most people will take a decade as a long enough time horizon to judge this on. I don't have a lot of evidence for this, but consider an example: Tesla Roadster came out in 2008 (the first Li-Ion road-legal electric car in the US) and the electric vehicle sales did not start going up consistently YoY till about 2021. By that time, there were enough variants, and reliability data that people were willing to ditch the old normal.

So let's say we have another decade and a bit of human programming as a viable career option for the masses. The current generation of programmers would be towards the middle or end of their careers by then. The new generation of programmers will have come up in the world of LLM-generated code being normal and maybe even the norm. These folks are currently pre-teens. They will have lots of time to adapt to this world. I am OK with this.

I am also okay with LLMs being the way most code is generated. What I am not okay with is that this power (foundational models) living in the hands of few companies. I really hope that LLMs become commoditised and companies like Anthropic and Mistral have to find other ways to make money than renting out their models. Then I can go live out my life hand-building programs as a hobby, just like I did for years before I got paid for it.

comments.author: nolan
comments.text: I suppose two reasons: 1) The fact that AI coding tools exist kind of takes the wind out of my sails; it makes hand-coding feel wasteful or even indulgent. 2) Unlike a handmade scarf (say, as a gift for a loved one), I don't think most people care whether an app is vibe-coded or not – they just care if it works.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
I think you’re pointing at something real. Maybe that fades over time, maybe it doesn’t - I hope it does for you and me both. My dad still hacks on his old car.

Most users never cared how something was coded, only whether it works and feels good. The appreciation of coding itself was always pretty niche, and I suspect that niche will survive.

The interesting shift to me is that more people can now participate in building things. I’m seeing low/no-tech folks vibe-code apps, enjoy the process, and create things others enjoy too - which feels closer to “craft” again, just with a different audience.

Optimistically, this looks like a bit of a creator resurgence. Maybe that’s naive, but I’m hopeful.

comments.author: ap
comments.text:
It’s wasteful only if working code is your sole goal. The question is whether you value your understanding of how the code works, which can only be had as a byproduct of manual creation of the code. The ability to understand code itself is defensible by the same arguments by which foundational research is advocated for.

I suppose what has changed is that understanding the code has now become optional and thus opened up a choice (which not making is, as always, itself a choice).
